sections.title: Name the question first
sections.body: Start with the decision the partner must support: diagnose a loss, prioritise a backlog, review a release, prepare a content plan or define implementation. A clear question prevents generic research from consuming the scope.

sections.title: Describe the site, market and audience
sections.body: Name the domain, relevant routes, country, language, searcher, business objective and commercially important pages. Add previous work, migrations, tracking changes or campaigns that could affect interpretation.

sections.title: List what can block delivery
sections.body: State platform limits, access gaps, legal review, developer availability, content approvals, launch dates and client sensitivities. Constraints are part of the decision, not administrative detail to hide.

sections.title: State available evidence and permissions
sections.body: List analytics, search performance, CMS, crawl, staging or profile access. Explain what is unavailable. Credentials should stay in appropriate systems; the brief records the boundary rather than copying secrets.

sections.title: Define format, brand and definition of done
sections.body: Name the outputs, file type, client-facing treatment, required sections, audience, deadline, review owner and verification check. Separate advice, implementation, presentation and post-release checking.

sections.title: Protect a bounded scope
sections.body: List exclusions and ask the partner to return assumptions and open questions before deep research. For recurring work, maintain a dated change log. New discoveries can be recorded without silently becoming promises.
